name: Skin-only facelift
lead: A skin-only facelift is a form of rhytidectomy in which the surgeon lifts and redrapes the facial skin and removes the excess, without separately tightening or repositioning deeper layers such as the SMAS (superficial musculoaponeurotic system) or facial muscles. It is used to smooth jowls and loose skin along the lower face so the jawline looks firmer and the face looks younger.[1][2]

It is the oldest and simplest approach to facelifting, and it is contrasted in the surgical literature with SMAS, deep-plane and composite techniques. Wikipedia reports that it has fewer complications and quicker recovery than deeper procedures, and that it may suit a simple jowl lift in patients roughly 35 to 45 years old.[1][2]

The American Society of Plastic Surgeons describes a facelift generally as a restorative surgery that improves sagging skin, deeper folds beside the nose and mouth, jowls and loose neck skin, while not stopping aging. No controlled trials of the skin-only technique are listed in these sources, and longevity figures come from encyclopedia summaries.[3]

angle.text: The procedure tightens the skin envelope of the lower face and neck, visibly reducing jowling and slack. Because deeper layers are left alone, recovery is lighter than for deeper lifts; results are reported to last about 5 to 10 years.

paras: In a skin-only facelift only the skin is elevated and pulled; the SMAS and muscles are not mobilised. It may involve removing a simple ellipse of skin or raising a larger skin flap, and surgeons are described as needing skill to judge how much skin to remove and in which direction to pull.[1] Facelifts are usually performed under general anaesthesia or deep sedation and are often combined with eyelid surgery.[1] Facelift surgery is often paired with brow lifts, eyelid surgery, fat transfer or fillers, and skin treatments such as laser, peels and dermabrasion.[3]

Wikipedia lists the traditional SMAS facelift, deep-plane, composite, mid-face, mini, subperiosteal and thread lifts, and the MACS lift among other approaches. The deep-plane lift moves skin and deeper tissue as one unit, while the skin-only lift relies on skin tension, which is why the SMAS-based methods became standard after the 1970s.[2] Traditional facelift recovery is cited as 3 to 4 weeks versus 2 to 3 for the MACS lift, with mini and skin-only lifts described as having less downtime.[2]

Facelift surgery between about 1900 and 1970 was essentially cutaneous: surgeons pulled the skin and cut away the excess. Eugen Holländer reportedly performed the first facelift in Berlin in 1901, and Charles Miller of Chicago wrote the first textbook on facial cosmetic surgery in 1907.[1][2] SMAS-based techniques followed in the 1970s after Tord Skoog introduced subfascial dissection and Mitz and Peyronie described the SMAS in 1976, and later deep-plane and volumetric approaches became widespread.[1][2]

Facelift complications described in general include haematoma (the most common, usually within 24 hours), injury to the greater auricular or facial nerve branches, skin necrosis, scarring, hair loss at incisions and, rarely, infection. Smoking raises skin necrosis risk about 12-fold, and hypertension and diabetes are also listed as risk factors.[1][2] Excess skin removal or skin-tension-dependent closure can produce a windswept appearance or displace the ears and earlobes.[1][2]

card.summary: Lifting and trimming just the skin of the face; the oldest, simplest facelift, with milder recovery and a shorter-lived result than deeper techniques.
card.note: Surgical procedure; reported longevity figures come from summaries, not controlled trials.

quick.overview:
A skin-only facelift lifts the facial skin and removes the excess without working on the SMAS or muscle underneath. It was the standard facelift for most of the early 20th century and remains described as a simpler option for mild jowling.

Encyclopedia summaries say it has fewer complications and a faster recovery than deeper facelifts, but results are reported to last around 5 to 10 years. No dedicated trials were found.
quick.mechanism: The surgeon raises a skin flap, pulls it in a chosen direction, trims the surplus and closes the incision, relying on the skin itself to hold the result [1].
quick.risks: General facelift risks include haematoma, nerve injury, skin necrosis, scarring and infection; smoking, hypertension and diabetes raise risk. Skin-only technique is described as having fewer complications than deeper variants, but excessive skin tension can distort the ears or give a windswept look [1].
